summary_for_user:
Kamlesh's old resume had all the right experience buried where nobody reads it. A recruiter spends about ten seconds on a CV. On the old one, those ten seconds showed a name, a skills list, and an employer with no dates at all - you had to reach page two before you learned when or where he worked, and his best material (the Best Performer Award, the 100% sprint coverage, the 40% faster regression runs, the 50% coverage lift) was sitting on page two too.

The new version moves the evidence up. His years of experience are now in the line under his name. Two dated jobs appear on page one, so the reader immediately sees a continuous record from August 2022. The two strongest numbers are in the opening paragraph, and the award and the sprint-coverage win are the first two bullets of his current job. Each job also ends with a plain list of the product modules he tested, which is what recruiter search tools actually match on.

Nothing new was invented. Every line traces back to his existing resume, and in several places the wording was pulled BACK to what he originally wrote - "JavaScript (Basics)" instead of plain JavaScript, "contributed to" the hackathon system instead of "designed" it, and the removal of a claim about testing unauthorised access that he never made. Small exaggerations like that are what collapse in a screening call.

Four blanks marked [CONFIRM: ...] remain. The important one is the employer name on his 2022-2024 job - he must fill that in before sending the file anywhere.

lens_top_changes.lens: Hiring-manager credibility — read adversarially by a QA hiring manager screening ~60 resumes/week, looking for a reason to say no in under 10 seconds
top: Put a date range on the employment block — and get it there structurally, by promoting Priority Financial Network (Feb 2024 - Present) and Cortex EDI (Aug 2022 - Jan 2024) into `experience` entries in their own right. One move fixes three things: every block gets the `dates` the ATS needs to compute his 4 years (without it he can parse as 0 and never appear in a 3-6 year search), the strongest content keeps real bullets instead of being flattened into a prose paragraph, and the dated material moves to the top of the page where the 10-second scan actually lands. Use `[CONFIRM: start Mon YYYY] - Present` on the Superworks header and `[CONFIRM: same employer for both projects?]` where the source is ambiguous.

Give every percentage a denominator or a before/after pair — do not delete any of them. "40%" becomes "from [CONFIRM: X] to [CONFIRM: Y] minutes wall-clock" with cross-browser split out as a separate coverage claim (it adds work, it does not save time — a good interviewer will catch the contradiction). "100% sprint coverage" becomes "all [CONFIRM: N] user stories accepted in the sprint" and leads Key Achievements so the verifiable Best Performer Award 2025 carries it. "50% coverage improvement" becomes "from [CONFIRM: N] to [CONFIRM: N] automated test cases". Add at least four absolute numbers (suite size, test-case count, release cadence, team size) — three denominator-free percentages and zero absolutes is the recognised signature of an inflated resume, and it discredits his true claims along with the loose ones.

Add the missing screening facts and stop leading with commodity content. Missing and cheap to fix: LinkedIn and GitHub URLs (no GitHub on an automation resume leaves 'did he build it or just run it?' unanswered), graduation year and branch (absent year reads as a hidden backlog and blocks year-of-passing filters), notice period and location preference, and team size/sole-QA context. At the same time, cut 'Results-driven' and the four table-stakes bullets (stand-ups, Git, 'multiple product modules', 'to ensure product quality'), delete 'GenAI Tools Awareness' — 'awareness' is read as an admission of no depth — and promote MCP out of the middle of a PFN bullet into the skill line with a concrete use. MCP is the rarest thing on his resume and is currently the best-hidden.
